headline: Committee reviews Warming Shelter and Project HOPE updates, and discusses the Bangor Homeless Response System Roadmap.
summary: The committee will hear updates on the Warming Shelter, Project HOPE, and committee appointments. Members will also discuss the Bangor Homeless Response System Roadmap and plan the agenda for the next meeting on Oct 27th.

Purpose 
Reframe Bangor’s homelessness landscape as an end-to-end response 
system. The roadmap identifies existing resources, the populations reached 
at each stage, and the points where limited capacity or missing connections 
allow people to remain homeless or return to homelessness. 
 
Executive takeaway 
Bangor has a broad provider network across outreach, shelter, health care, housing and coordination. The central issue 
identified on page 5 is not simply the absence of services. It is the system’s limited capacity, uneven accessibility and wea k 
continuity between stages. 
STRENGTH 
Multiple entry points and experienced 
providers 
BOTTLENECK 
Shelter, day-space, transportation and 
case-management capacity 
PRIORITY 
Build continuity from first contact through 
housing retention 
 
Prepared from page 5, “Landscape for Addressing Homelessness in Bangor,” in the September 22, 2026 Advisory Committee packet.
Bangor Homelessness Response Roadmap  |  Advisory Committee Working Document

2. Who Is Helped, and Where Gaps Appear 
A. Prevention 
WHO IS REACHED 
Households facing eviction; students 
experiencing housing instability; older 
adults and low-income renters at risk; 
people with complex health needs with 
current insufficient housing; Young adults 
leaving foster care 
RESOURCES IN PLACE 
• City of Bangor eviction prevention 
• Hope House / Preble Street prevention 
• Bangor Area Shelter prevention 
• McKinney-Vento student support 
• Bangor Housing and other housing 
providers 
• Shaw House eviction prevention 
GAPS / PRESSURE POINTS 
• Rising housing costs for people on 
fixed incomes 
• Limited affordable inventory 
• Credit, criminal-background and pet 
barriers 
• Pet barriers 
B. Street Outreach and Engagement 
WHO IS REACHED 
People living outdoors, in encampments or 
otherwise disconnected from traditional 
services. 
RESOURCES IN PLACE 
• PATH and HOME Team 
• City outreach and case management 
• Street Plus in the downtown area 
• Options Team and BCAT 
• PCHC street medicine 
GAPS / PRESSURE POINTS 
• People are geographically scattered 
• Case sizes reduce contact frequency 
• Workforce hiring, pay, training and 
burnout challenges 
C. Emergency Shelter 
WHO IS REACHED 
People needing immediate overnight 
safety, including adults and youth. 
RESOURCES IN PLACE 
• Hope House 
• Bangor Area Shelter 
• Shaw House 
• Warming-center planning and funding 
GAPS / PRESSURE POINTS 
• Shelters are at capacity 
• No family shelter 
• People with pets or other barriers may 
not fit existing options 
• Shelters do not have resources to take 
people with complex health needs
Bangor Homelessness Response Roadmap  |  Advisory Committee Working Document 
2. Who Is Helped, and Where Gaps Appear (continued) 
D. Daytime Services and Basic Needs 
WHO IS REACHED 
People who are unsheltered, shelter 
residents during daytime hours, and 
individuals seeking a safe place to connect 
with services. 
RESOURCES IN PLACE 
• Bangor Area Shelter 
• Bangor Public Library 
• The Well during winter 
• Brick Church two days per week 
• BARN and Together Place 
• Hope House day access for shelter 
residents 
GAPS / PRESSURE POINTS 
• No centralized service-navigation hub 
• Limited low-barrier day space 
• Laundry and shower access 
• Reliable phones and immediate 
transportation 
E. Health, Behavioral Health and Recovery 
WHO IS REACHED 
People with medical needs, severe mental 
illness, substance-use disorders, and 
specialized needs. 
RESOURCES IN PLACE 
• PCHC street medicine 
• CHCS mobile crisis unit 
• Planned crisis receiving center 
• Domestic-violence supports through 
Partners for Peace 
• Veteran supports through VA and Preble 
Street 
GAPS / PRESSURE POINTS 
• People leaving detox may return to 
homelessness 
• Difficulty obtaining support or 
hospitalization for severe mental illness 
• Insufficient long-term stabilization and 
tenancy support 
F. Transitional and Permanent Housing 
WHO IS REACHED 
People moving from shelter or unsheltered 
homelessness into structured, supportive 
or independent housing. 
RESOURCES IN PLACE 
• PCHC, Leading the Way and Wellspring 
transitional housing 
• Bangor Housing, CHOM, Theresa’s 
Place, Waterworks and Maine Hall 
• DHHS / Preble Street / City permanent 
supportive housing 
• Project HOPE and Community Care 
Housing Support Services in process 
GAPS / PRESSURE POINTS 
• Not enough housing for demand 
• Housing barriers involving credit, 
criminal records and pets 
• Skills developed for outdoor survival may 
not translate to tenancy 
• Need for intensive, ongoing support after 
placement

Immediate safety and

4. Committee Action Roadmap 
A practical next step is to assign each gap to a workstream, establish the baseline, and identify which organization is 
responsible for convening the response. The actions below are recommendations developed from the mapped gaps.  
0–90 DAYS Clarify and organize 
• Validate provider names, eligibility, hours, referral paths and 
current capacity 
• Create one public-facing resource directory and one 
provider-facing referral map 
• Define baseline measures for shelter demand, unsheltered 
outreach, housing placements and returns to homelessness 
• Name a lead convener for each priority gap 
• Develop and recommend a communication plan for the City 
to share the resources available.  
 
3–9 MONTHS Close access and coordination gaps 
• Develop a service-hub / low-barrier day-space concept 
• Identify interim options for family shelter and winter overflow 
• Develop transportation coverage options for evenings, 
weekends and urgent appointments 
• Create formal handoff protocols for detox, crisis care, shelter 
and housing placement 
 
9–24 MONTHS Expand capacity and sustain housing 
• Advance additional affordable and supportive housing 
• Build a long-term funding model for intensive housing 
navigation and retention 
• Strengthen landlord participation and barrier-mitigation tools 
• Adopt a workforce strategy addressing hiring, training, 
compensation and burnout 
 
Questions the Advisory Committee should be able to answer 
• Where can a person go today, after 5:00 p.m., or on a weekend for shelter, navigation and basic needs? 
• Which populations have no workable shelter option, particularly families and people with pets? 
• Where do referrals fail because of eligibility, capacity, transportation or communication barriers? 
• What ongoing support is available after housing placement, and for how long? 
• Which gaps require new resources, and which can be improved through coordination or clearer public information? 
 
 
Recommended committee framing 
Bangor should evaluate success not only by the number of programs available, but by 
whether a person can move through the system without losing contact, waiting indefinitely 
at a bottleneck, or returning to homelessness after treatment or housing placement.
